title: What does FFmpeg -ac 1 do to stereo?
fullTitle: FFmpeg -ac 1 Averages Stereo. Out-of-Phase Audio Vanishes

scenes.narration: You turn a stereo file into mono with FFmpeg: dash a c one. Is the mono file as loud as the stereo one? We make four stereo files, and turn each into mono three ways.

Each source is a two second, four hundred forty hertz tone in the left channel, at minus eight d B F S. The right channel is the same, or inverted, or silent, or a different tone. We read each file two ways. The astats filter, and the raw sixteen bit samples.
captions: Right channel: same, inverted, silent, different.
Two readers: astats, and raw samples.

scenes.narration: When both channels are identical, dash a c one changes nothing. The peak stays at minus seven point nine six d B. This is the case most people test, and it hides what follows.

When only the left channel has sound, dash a c one averages it with silence. The peak falls by six point oh two d B, to minus thirteen point nine eight. A podcast with one active microphone ends up half as loud.
captions: Only left has sound: 6 dB quieter.

scenes.narration: When the right channel is the left, inverted, the average is zero. Both readers see nothing at all: minus infinity. Digital silence, from a file that sounded fine in stereo.
captions: Right = inverted left: average is zero.

scenes.narration: Pan with c zero equals c zero keeps the left channel at its own level, in all four sources. Pan with c zero equals c zero plus c one adds the channels: identical channels gain six d B, and out-of-phase still cancels. The right mix depends on the recording.
captions: c0+c1 adds: +6 dB on identical channels.

scenes.narration: Dash a c one is an average. Check the loudness, and check the phase, before you trust a mono file. Not tested: five point one downmix, real recordings, and other builds beyond the two named.
